I didn't find a direct NREL PVWatts result for December average daily insolation on a tilted array in Albuquerque or Santa Fe. The closest data points are below, and none is an official PVWatts output for both cities.

- **Albuquerque, forum-posted PVWatts-style run (undated):** Using lat 35.05, a 35° fixed tilt gives about 5.14 kWh/m²/day for December. A 50° tilt gives 5.61 for December in the same table. The forum post doesn't say which PVWatts version was used, so treat these as indicative only.
- **Albuquerque, third-party site (NASA POWER data, not PVWatts):** Winter output is about 3.77 kWh per day per kW. That is a seasonal average, not a December tilted-array figure.
- **Santa Fe, third-party site (NASA POWER data, not PVWatts):** Winter output falls to about 3.85 kWh per day per kW. Again, this is a seasonal average and not a December tilted-array value.
- **New Mexico, a blog post citing PVWatts v8:** One article says December is the weakest month at 4.4 PSH, and its methodology lists NREL PVWatts v8 / NSRDB for Albuquerque with a 1 kW reference system, fixed roof mount, 20° tilt, 180° azimuth, 14% losses. The snippet doesn't clearly tie the 4.4 figure to Albuquerque, so I wouldn't rely on it without checking.

For an authoritative December number, run PVWatts directly at pvwatts.nrel.gov for each city's coordinates, using your chosen tilt and azimuth, and read the monthly "Solar Radiation" column. Note that PVWatts reports the value on the tilted plane. Santa Fe's coordinates are about 35.62°N, 105.87°W, and Albuquerque's are about 35.08°N, 106.65°W.

Links: [{"title":"Solar Lighting: Making Steps Off-Grid towards a Sustainable Future","url":"https://continuingeducation.bnpmedia.com/courses/selux/solar-lighting-making-steps-offgrid-towards-a-sustainable-future/9"},{"title":"Getting the most out of your solar array","url":"https://www.greentechrenewables.com/node/45793"},{"title":"Complete Off-Grid Solar System Design Guide","url":"https://muhammed.portlandiaelectric.supply/blogs/energy-solutions/complete-off-grid-solar-system-design-guide"},{"title":"Back to Blog","url":"https://www.surgepv.com/blog/off-grid-solar-system-sizing-calculator"},{"title":"off grid solar power site suitability selection considerations","url":"https://www.solar-wind.co.uk/info/off-grid-solar-power-site-suitability-selection-considerations"},{"title":"How to Go Completely Off-Grid with Solar: A Realistic Roadmap","url":"https://shopsolarkits.com/blogs/learning-center/how-to-go-off-grid-with-solar"},{"title":"Solar Pv System Sizing Interactive Calculator","url":"https://www.firgelliauto.com/es/blogs/calculators/solar-pv-system-sizing-calculator"},{"title":"how many solar panels for a cabin","url":"https://www.thegreenwatt.com/how-many-solar-panels-for-a-cabin/"},{"title":"samplecontents.library.ph","url":"https://samplecontents.library.ph/en-practical_action/Energy/Solar%20energy/off-grid-solar-install-manual/page29.html"}]

The results back the core method: size an off-grid array to the worst solar month, and tilt steeper for winter. The sources agree on the broad approach but differ on details.

- **Design month:** One source says off-grid systems are sized for the critical design month, the one with the lowest radiation and longest nights, which for a northern site like New York State is December. Off grid systems are most concerned with optimizing tilt angle to achieve the highest minimum irradiation value during the critical design month. Several vendor guides say annual averages underestimate winter shortfalls. One gives a December example in northern Idaho where production is about half the annual average.
- **Sizing formula:** One vendor guide divides daily load in watt-hours by winter peak sun hours and then by a 0.75 derating factor to cover wiring, controller, battery, inverter, and temperature losses. Array Size: W = Daily load (Wh) ÷ Winter PSH ÷ 0.75. The 0.75 factor accounts for real-world losses.
- **Tilt rule:** The latitude + 15° rule appears in several sources. One says for sites in the northern hemisphere (to optimise tilt angle for the winter) is to add approx 15 degrees to the latitude. Another frames it as Winter loads: Tilt angle equals latitude plus 15 degrees, with latitude for year-round loads and latitude minus 15 for summer loads. A third notes that tilt angle optimization can increase winter collection by 40-60% compared to horizontal mounting, though this comes at the expense of summer generation.
- **Tools:** NREL PVWatts is the most commonly recommended tool for checking monthly production at a given tilt. One guide says set the array tilt to latitude, and read the December production column.
- **Caveats:** The sources are mostly vendor blogs, and their figures don't fully agree. A peak-sun-hours table gives a Seattle winter range of 1.5–2.0, while another guide puts the Pacific Northwest near 3.5 on an annual basis. A European manual also gives a different winter tilt formula (latitude + 20°) for temperate zones, so treat latitude + 15° as a rule of thumb and verify with PVWatts or Global Solar Atlas for the specific site.

content.text:
## First-principles sizing

**Step 1 — Design month, not annual average.** An off-grid system has to survive the worst month, not the typical one. At 35°N that's December/January: shortest days, lowest sun angle. Sizing off an annual-average insolation number is the single most common off-grid sizing mistake — it leaves you short exactly when nights are longest and (if you use any resistive heat or heat-tape) loads are highest.

**Step 2 — Winter solar resource at this latitude.** For a ground-mount array tilted steeply for winter (tilt ≈ latitude + 15°, so ~50° here), PVWatts-style runs for Albuquerque/Santa Fe (35–35.6°N) put December output around **5.0–5.6 effective peak-sun-hours (PSH)/day** on the tilted plane. High-desert NM is unusually good for this — clear, dry, high-elevation skies mean winter insolation doesn't collapse the way it does in cloudier climates at the same latitude. I'll design to **5.0 PSH** as a conservative round number; a flatter, roof-pitch tilt (~20°) would cut this to roughly 4.4 PSH, so tilt angle matters a lot here — don't mount flush with a low-pitch roof if you can avoid it.

**Step 3 — System derate.** Real losses between "panel nameplate watts" and "watt-hours actually in the battery": MPPT conversion, wiring resistance, dust/soiling, temperature derate, battery charge efficiency. Combined, that's conventionally **0.75** for an off-grid system (vs. ~0.85 for grid-tied, which has fewer conversion stages).

**Step 4 — Array size.**
Array (W) = Daily load (Wh) ÷ Design PSH ÷ derate
= 1500 ÷ 5.0 ÷ 0.75 ≈ **400 W** bare minimum to break even in December.

That's a minimum, with zero margin. Add 25–40% for panel degradation over a 25-year warranty life, snow/dust events, and because a "rough estimate" load number is far more likely to be revised upward than downward (see caveat below). That lands you at **≈550–650 W**, and practically you'd buy in standard increments — **two 300–400 W panels (≈600–800 W total)** is the realistic target, not the theoretical 400 W floor.

**Step 5 — Battery: autonomy and depth of discharge.**
- Usable energy needed = daily load × autonomy days = 1.5 kWh × 3 = **4.5 kWh usable**.
- LiFePO4 tolerates deep cycling far better than lead-acid, but for good cycle life (thousands of cycles) design to **80% DoD**, not 100%.
- Nameplate capacity = 4.5 ÷ 0.80 = **5.6 kWh minimum**.

Round to a standard product size: a single 48 V/100 Ah LiFePO4 pack (≈5.1 kWh) or stacked smaller units gets you there. Given the same load-underestimate risk as above, **6–10 kWh nameplate** is the practical target rather than the bare 5.6 kWh floor.

## Bottom line

| | Bare minimum (computed) | Practical recommendation (with margin) |
|---|---|---|
| Array | ~400 W | **600–800 W** |
| Battery (LiFePO4, 3-day autonomy, 80% DoD) | ~5.6 kWh | **6–10 kWh** |

## The load estimate is the thing to re-check

Everything above scales linearly with the 1.5 kWh/day number, and that figure is light for **year-round, 2-adult occupancy**. 1.5 kWh/day is plausible only for LED lighting + phone/laptop charging + a hand- or gravity-fed water system, with no electric refrigeration, no well pump, and no internet hardware running continuously. The moment you add any one of:
- a 12V/DC or efficient compressor fridge (~0.5–1.5 kWh/day),
- a well pump (~0.2–0.5 kWh/day, more if deep),
- Starlink or similar satellite internet run 24/7 (often **0.5–1.5 kWh/day alone**),
- any circulation pump for a wood/propane heating system,

...you're well past 1.5 kWh/day — realistically into 3–5 kWh/day territory for a genuinely livable year-round cabin. I'd suggest doing a proper appliance-by-appliance watt-hour audit before finalizing hardware purchases, since doubling the load estimate doubles both array and battery requirements directly. If you want, I can help you build that load table next.

Sources:
- [New Mexico peak sun hours](https://www.thegreenwatt.com/new-mexico-peak-sun-hours/)
- [Optimising array angle (forum PVWatts discussion, Albuquerque tilt comparison)](https://forum.solar-electric.com/discussion/comment/85080)
- [Complete Off-Grid Solar System Design Guide](https://muhammed.portlandiaelectric.supply/blogs/energy-solutions/complete-off-grid-solar-system-design-guide)
- [How many solar panels for a cabin](https://www.thegreenwatt.com/how-many-solar-panels-for-a-cabin/)
